name: Dome Jiotto Caspita
description:
The Dome Jiotto Caspita is one of Japan's most ambitious and exotic automotive projects—a mid-engine supercar concept that challenged the established European supercar hierarchy in the late 1980s. Created by Dome, a respected Japanese racing constructor known for their Group C and Le Mans prototypes, the Caspita (Italian for 'good grief') was unveiled in 1989 as a fully functional prototype that showcased Japan's capability to build world-class exotic automobiles.

Beneath the striking wedge-shaped bodywork, styled by renowned Italian designer Emanuele Nicosia, sat a highly tuned Subaru-derived flat-six boxer engine. This 3.5-liter twin-turbocharged powerplant produced an impressive 451 horsepower and 512 Nm of torque, mated to a 5-speed manual transmission driving the rear wheels. The use of a Subaru-based engine explains the Subaru badges sometimes associated with the car, as Dome partnered with Subaru for the powertrain development.

The Caspita featured advanced aerodynamics with a remarkably low coefficient of drag, active aerodynamic elements, and a sophisticated chassis designed using Dome's extensive racing experience. With its lightweight construction targeting around 1,470 kg and exceptional power output, the Caspita was claimed to achieve 0-100 km/h in just 3.8 seconds with a top speed exceeding 340 km/h—performance figures that would have made it one of the fastest cars in the world.

Despite its impressive specifications and the technical expertise behind it, the Dome Jiotto Caspita never reached production. Only a handful of prototypes were built, making it one of the most exclusive and intriguing Japanese supercars ever created. The Caspita remains a fascinating 'what if' in automotive history—a glimpse of what Japan could have achieved in the exotic supercar market.
